I don't think I can further emphasize how mediocre this game is. I would not say this game is worth $40, I got it on sale, and I have about 2 hours of game play per dollar I spent. I have 100% completed this game, challenges and all. Has some major flaws, but it's not a full game. Short review: 6.5/10, But not damnable. I recommend it b/c it is fun, It just missed the mark in a few areas. And, tbh, I would play through this game again with a friend or even for fun. It's simple FarCry fun. With that being said, If you like FarCry, buy this on sale, you won't regret it. Also, SPOILERS.

Things I liked:
-Has a "better" ending than FarCry 5. (Albeit debatable.)
-Concludes FarCry 5's story line. 
-Visually appealing 
-Tried something new. (Although most of these changes I would be happy if they NEVER came to light again.
-TIMBER. (And car rides with him.)

Things I had mixed feelings about:
-Antagonists: Mickie and Lou are very, very bland for FarCry villains. Honestly, they get a 6/10. 
-Joseph helps you, and doesn't act like he did in FarCry 5. Both in a good way and in a bad way.
-Leveling: Leveling is SUPER easy. Playing as I did will result in max stats and gear halfway through.
-Looting: There are two situations you run into regarding loot. A.) Ah shit... I have no materials. Or B.) Having 
  so much loot, you don't know what to do with it.
-Sheer grind for 100%: There are several things a "completion-ist" would want to do to feel like he/she 
  100%'ed the game. It's almost agonizing. 
-Hope county?: I understand that several nuclear bombs went off, but other than a few locations, it didn't 
  feel like Hope County. Might be just me.
- FUCKING PINK!: I'm sorry, but when does radiation = pink? I get it, its different and all that, but it feels off.
- Those who had a serious role in FarCry 5 are tossed aside, while side characters in FarCry 5 become main 
   characters in this game. (Not going to go into detail because spoilers... if you care.)
-Absent Characters. (Jess Black, Cheeseburger, Peaches, Adeline Drubman, etc.) Some characters are 
  revealed to be dead, but some are unexplained or flat-out missing in this game. 

Things I didn't like/hated:
-Guns: Crafting weapons is way, way, way to costly. 123 titanium for a pistol? That doesn't even 
  make any sense. Also, some weapons are vastly superior to others. Bows are better than .50 sniper riflers in 
  this game, due to the armor mechanics. 
-Armor: Your enemies have armor now. So, some can take a bullet/arrow to the face and still keep fighting. 
 Some helmets may save your life depending on the distance, caliber, etc; but a normal helmet shouldn't save 
  your life from a .50 Caliber BMG to the face from like 100yds away. Sorry... YOUR DEAD. Also, Bows are 
 somehow able to go through chest-plates with ease, but helmets only shatter from arrows. What gives?
-Enemy ranks/gear ranks: So, you have four ranks. Common, Uncommon, Legendary, and Elite. Self 
  Explanatory. But, elite enemies and to a certain degree, Legendary enemies, are perhaps a little too strong 
  in my opinion. Not saying they're too hard to kill, but an average person in motocross gear should normally 
  die from a few rounds from an MG42 at close range... Especially if some of those rounds fired are 
  headshots...  
-Guns/Fangs/Bows for Hire: My god. They FUCKED Guns for hire in this game... All of these characters have 
  three tiers, they all need 40 kills to reach the third tier. Also, sometimes they just stop moving or have fits 
  of confusion for no reason. My guess, their path-finding ability is all fucked up... Only three are worth using. 
  
  -Pastor Jerome has a shotgun, and throws Molotovs. In concept, this sounds good, but he shoots his 
    shotgun from too far away to do any real damage, and I've seen him kill himself with his own molotovs. 
    1/10. 
   -Carmina Rye has an Ar, and throws dynamite. She can't aim worth shit. She gets to throw three sticks of 
     dynamite at her third tier.  2/10. Only because I haven't seen her killing herself with her own dynamite.
     Wouldn't be surprised though... 
   -Gina is fucking awesome. She swings her MG42 like a baseball bat in stealth mode, and is accurate with 
     her LMG when detected. Also, she gets infinite ammo, and explosive ammo when she reaches third tier 
     Seriously, my third favorite Gun for Hire in this game. 9/10
   -Nana is the best human Gun for Hire in this game. She's quiet, and she's lethal. 2nd tier grants her the 
    ability to see through smoke. And her 3rd tier allows her shots to NEGATE COVER. THIS GRANNY GETS 
    WALL-HACKS BRO. 10/10
   -The Judge, is disappointing. He/She gets a bow. He/She has difficulty when detected or dealing with high
    ranking enemies. He/She gives immunity to wildlife in the 2nd tier. And Tri-shot in the 3rd tier. He/She is 
    limited in range, and sometimes only destroys armor, setting off alarms. EXTREMELY ANNOYING TO WORK 
    WITH AT TIMES. However, his/her tri-shot does allow him/her to kill higher ranking enemies. He/She is still 
    fucked if they're detected. 5/10.
   -Hurk: OH HURK... You actually made me laugh in this game, yet you're so shit... Hurk gets a MAC-10 and a 
    rocket Launcher. He can't aim worth shit, and he takes forever killing individual targets. He has no stealth 
    mode, just balls-to-the-wall loud. He gets faster reloads on his 2nd tier, and vehicle tracking on his 3rd tier. 
    Just as fucking useless and is as bad as Pastor Jerome. But, his only saving grace is vehicular 
    destruction. 4/10.
   -Timber is the best Guns/Fangs for Hire in this game. Not very good at killing, but TIMBER SEES
    EVERYTHING. Enemies, friendlies, loot, guns, materials, the list goes on. Also, he will take the 
    attention of animals when you're fighting them in the third tier. Super useful Albeit not very lethal. Timber 
    is a truly good boy. 10/10. Also he can sit in the car with you. THX UBISOFT. 
   -Lastly, Horatio. Horatio is the CHEAPEST Fangs for Hire/Guns for Hire character EVER CREATED. Horatio 
    can SELF REVIVE at his 2nd tier. Literally, just send him in a compound, and just wait, he'll get it done. And 
    his 3rd tier allows him to destroy anything in his way. Literally the god of destruction. However, Timber is 
    still better because Timber isn't an OP piece of shit unlike Horatio. 7/10, only for being so damn OP. 

-Silent Protagonist. 
-Forgettable Characters. 
-Short story. There are 22 missions total in this game. If I wanted to beat the game as fast as possible, I'd 
  imagine it'd take no more than 10 hours; 15 hours tops. 
-Expeditions: They only exist to pad the lack of content, get more resources, and make it ever so slightly 
  harder to 100% this game. I get the appeal, but I don't like it. 
-Upgradable perks: Some perks are able to be upgraded, stacking the effectiveness of the perk. But, this 
  could allow someone to max out a perk like ammo holding, which allows them to carry upwards of 
  thousands of rounds of ammo at once. 
-"God perks": Once you reach a certain point in the game, you get special powers such as a double jump, a 
  sneak ability, a rage ability, and a take-down that replenishes energy for the other abilities and replenishes 
  health. Making the game even MORE easier. 
-Not being able to modify/kit out you weapons: You can't choose attachments in this game, you're stuck 
  with what the game gives you. It's not bad, but its not great either. I enjoyed the freedom of customization. 
  (although some customizations in FarCry 5 were absurd. I.E. Suppressors on belt-fed machine guns.)



That's it, that's my in-depth analysis review of this game. I would say if you enjoy FarCry games, or you want to know how this story ends, get the game and play it. At least you'll get to see how it ends. Otherwise, I feel like this game was decent for its price. But nothing more than decent. I hope this will be helpful to someone.

I feel like this game has me hating the antagonists for the wrong reasons.

You see, Fc5 had goals. It had characters who HAD goals that conflicted with other characters. Even Joseph could barely control his siblings at times. These twins, Mickey and Lou? I feel like someone spent ages coming up with backstory for them, making sure each sister had a distinctive personality and ambitions. Then someone told that writer that they already made the game with their first draft. Basically boiling them down to PINK SISTER ANGRY GRR and BLUE SISTER SMART  BUT ALSO ANGRY GRR. And this falls so flat because there isn't anything shown to the player that these characters are intimidating at the least. I would compare them to two girls whining to their father that they weren't able to kill the bad man/woman who keeps killing their friends. NOTHING is fleshed out about these two, most of their dialogue is through vague threats at the player and their lackeys for doing/not doing the thing that just happened. There was a point halfway through the game where you are FORCED to do something stupid with no alternative so the twins can be "Badass" with no repercussions. Again, I feel sorry for the writer/ writers that were on this game, because they obviously did not get enough time to write the story they wanted to write. 

Also, even placing an OPTION to buy guns with REAL money in these games is just insulting to the average player. Mobile game versions of monitization DO NOT belong in pc/console games. Its like having a man in a business suit ask you for 5 dollars to get you a soda from your fridge so you don't have to get it yourself; and if you don't pay he straps 20 pound weights to your ankles so you can "Feel like you deserve it."

Don't get this game. Not for the cut content nor the story. There is nothing here.

I enjoy playing this game overall, and I want to recommend it. However, I'm honestly disappointed by some really major elements, and can't give this a positive rating in good faith. If there were a neutral vote, I would select that instead. 

The game looks great and plays fluidly. The story, while perhaps a bit predictable, was honestly quite enjoyable and some characters (Joseph Seed!) were really well executed. The gameplay is good, but not surpassing. I'm fairly neutral on this, though it's failure to truly shine is probably due to the game's actual big problems.

Firstly, there's no weapon customization like in Far Cry 5, where you bought the base gun and then upgraded it by buying interchangeable parts for a custom build. In New Dawn, the guns are ranked along a series of tiers (this becomes a problem later; nothing inherently wrong there) and are completely unalterable. You want to put a scope on that silenced pistol instead of buying a scoped but unsilenced pistol? Nope. Not gonna happen. Wanna silence that sniper rifle, or attach a reflex sight to your shotgun? Still nope. This just reeks of lazy development and goes against the freedom of gameplay that Far Cry seems to be centered on. I no longer feel like my guns are my own or that my character is even vaguely self-sufficient, but rather as if I am an unintelligent, mostly useless individual who's really good at killing baddies but doesn't know how to mix weapon parts or even ask someone else to do it for him. It destroys immersion, character, and player agency with no clear benefit.

Secondly, they butchered my poor boy the perk system. Perks are stupidly annoying and grindy to get, requiring you to kill enemies not simply with A smg or shotgun, but with a Tier 1 smg, then a Tier 2 smg, all the way up to elite tier. Which is an issue because going back in the late game to running around with multiple loadouts of shitty guns is ultimately just unsatisfying, but an absolute requirement if you want to get all those sweet, sweet perk points. But Lo, and Behold! There is a reason they made perks so spread out and annoying to get- microtransactions! That's right, microtransactions toward a pay-to-win situation in a single-player game that's built specifically to frustrate you into buying perk points instead of grinding unhappily for them. On an already high-priced, AAA game. Absolutely disgusting, and I urge players who feel similarly about this not to buy this game. It looks beautiful, and I'm this close to recommending it, but I feel disgusted and gross every time I open my damn perks/challenges menu.  Just play Far Cry 5- it's really just the better game overall with better guns and cars, less pink, and it still has Joseph Seed.

If you don't own Far Cry 5, you really should buy that instead because it has a much better price-to-content ratio even at full price. Or even better get it on sale.

Waaay too expensive for what is essentially a Far Cry 5 mod - same graphics with new textures, same map only smaller, many of the same characters, very limited story content.
This game has a concerning amount of repeatable missions/tasks in lieu of proper crafted story missions as well - I hope this doesn't become the norm to pad out the game.
And many of the side-story missions you do get are basically 'defend the thing' or 'kill all enemies' and take about 5 minutes.

I would have liked to see them take the post-apocalypse theme further in terms of gameplay, because currently this is just literally normal guns with alternate skins, there's extremely little new or different here vs FC5 once you ignore the new art style.

(I know this is meant to be a quick & easy 'Far Cry 5.5' game but if you give it a big price tag I'm going to judge it like its a full instalment in the franchise)

For a fully priced game advertised as a sequel to Farcry 5, New Dawn feels like a bait and switch, it's absolutely more appropriate as an expansion. After the disasterous DLC packages for Farcry 5 it's also kind of insulting for the price.

New Dawn is literally a 1/3 piece of Far cry 5's map with some new objects and retextured locations, guns are 'DIY' style reskins and overall the game is the same with some half-assed enemy scaling and palette swaps. I would recommend at the $25 mark as a sort of FC5 epilogue, but this feels like content intended for the FC5 season pass thats been repackaged.

Far Cry New Dawn is the successor of Far Cry 5, and it carries along the backstory plus follows the same game mechanics from the previous title. It feels like a deluxe DLC of a game, but it’s decently impactful as a standalone game to enjoy and adore. There can be multiple natural improvements, but the published version is still fun to grind some hours on. Far Cry franchise always loves to experiment with uncanny twists in every title, whether it be crafting system, story twists or whole UI and environment.

[h1][b]Story without spoilers[/b][/h1]
[b]Continuity from previous title-[/b] After the nuke from Far Cry 5, People are living in bunkers under the devastated Hope County. After six years of retaining underground life, everyone is shocked to see nature self-healed. All the communities started the lifelong nourishing of humankind. The impact of Father (villainous priest) has decreased as he went missing for merely 17 years.

[b]Progressive plot-[/b] Even with all the peace and prosperity, there will always be a villainous group taking birth. Not much long after the beginning of prosperity, two twins, Lou and Mickey, violently attack Hope valley with their brutal groups. This peace turned into a warzone will present a variety of missions and twists all along with the story.

[h1][b]🎮Gameplay[/b][/h1]
Unlike traditional post-apocalypse slum sceneries, it presents you with an exceptionally vibrant open-world environment that includes multiple activities to conquer. It’s not just a survival game. It’s about survival, ambition, hunt and regaining multiple chores. You start in train wreckage while getting attacked by a violent mob known as Highwaymen. After escaping them, your journey of retaliation starts. You will craft some low to high tier weapons along with ambushing and winning over the outposts with your roster (co-op AI). Looting and Leveling up becomes easier as you progress through the gameplay.

Even though the primary missions contribute solely to your game progress, the side quests and hunting aren’t left alone. They are quite in-depth and immersive on their own. Attacking an armoured gang isn’t a straightforward task. That’s why you need an alias that you can trust. Doing side missions rewards you various items from rosters, materials, money and sometimes powerful gear. As every territory-based journey starts from a base camp, Prosperity acts as a home base for the peaceful community lead by Rush. You can upgrade various segments of the home base like cartography, garage, expedition and much more. They all require some hefty build materials, but in the end, they ease your gameplay in multiple ways.

You are never action deficient throughout the game. Even travelling through point A to point B will cause a random ambush ready to surprise you. The map is not very huge, but having an auto-drive feature can always act handy. Everything feels amusing and smooth. It’s a genuine blend of story and side quests grilled with an overdose of action. Hunting is not really in depth, but there’s a sufficient variety of animals to hunt and trade their skin for some extra bucks. Remember, it doesn’t matter whether you are on land or water. There will always be a ferocious animal ready to take you on. Not only that, there are some hybrid animals too that might stomp on your corpse pretty quick. Difficulty options were well-segmented to establish a do-able and challenge ratio.

[h1][b]📷Graphics[/b][/h1]
Easy 10/10. I don’t think there can be anyone disliking this piece of art. Not only the colours are vibrant, but the development is also top-notch. Enriched detailing and interaction with the environment always bind you to a strong thread of excitement. The blend of flower valley and devastating action somehow turned out pretty well. And the addition of Photo Mode just boosts your quench of capturing beautiful moments. You can also download extra texture packs to transform this heavenly environment into beyond imagination artwork.

[h1][b]📝Main Pros and Cons[/b][/h1]

[b]Pros-[/b]
[list]
    [*]Pleasant environment.
    [*]Concludes Far Cry 5
    [*]A useful dog companion who can sit with you in car. 
    [*]Smooth gameplay.
    [*]Good arsenal of weapon and armed vehicles.
    [*]Hunting and fishing.
[/list]

[b]Cons-[/b]
[list]
    [*]Dumb Roster AI.
    [*]Short story.
    [*]Silent Protagonist.
    [*]Not being able to modify/kit out you weapons.
    [*]Somehow bows impact more than a MLG.
[/list]

[h1][b]🏷️Tips to new players[/b][/h1]
As you don’t need separate equipment to tag your enemies, wander around the targeted place and scope of your gun to easily tag them. Roster AI is pretty dumb, so I suggest you either use Timber or Horatio. Initial missions want you to engage with outposts and ethanol convoys, so lockpick and vehicle repair perks will be most handy in the beginning.

[h1][b]✉️Miscellaneous Information[/b][/h1]
[b]Expedition-[/b]
Expedition probably acts as the difficulty factor of the game. Dropping you on the waypoint through a helicopter and makes you execute a solo raid against multiple enemies. Tag the package and escape the premises. Executing a successful expedition unlocks a higher tier mission next time. You can access them from the Prosperity home base.

[b]Similarities and Dissimilarities from Far Cry 5-[/b]
[list]
       [*][b]Similarities-[/b] Same silent protagonist who is experiencing the events instead of making a personality. Same location but with additional after nuke changes. The cult theme in addition to wildlife crafting. Roster features ascend again.
       [*][b]Dissimilarities-[/b]Far Cry New Dawn isn’t that free in the open-world aspect. You are just collecting resources for the home base. The story is not even half the size of Far Cry 5. 
[/list]

[b]Info about DLCs-[/b]
There are multiple DLCs available, ranging from high tier weapons, vehicles to fancy skins. Hurk legacy is probably the most useful one, as it provides you with a good calibre weapon and an effective gun mounted car. Rest DLCs are fine and not harmful to acquire. Texture DLC is free, so make sure to download it if your PC can fulfil the requirements.

[h1][b]😇Honest Rating[/b][/h1]
Being a fan of the Far Cry franchise, playing each new title is a fun experience. But calling Far Cry New Dawn a standalone game is hard to digest. It showcases more like a duplicate Far Cry 5 with map enhancements but half the content. The best part is probably the conclusion for Far Cry 5 ending, that you can experience in New Dawn. The asking price is too high, so please wait for a huge sale. If you never tried a Far Cry game and like this style of gameplay, then start with Far Cry 5. Otherwise, all the OG players should play this one too.

⭐️ Far Cry New Dawn — A Fun, Energetic Post‑Apocalyptic Adventure

Far Cry New Dawn takes the established Far Cry formula and reinvigorates it with vibrant visuals, exciting combat, engaging progression, and a surprising amount of heart. Set in the colorful, chaotic aftermath of Far Cry 5’s conclusion, New Dawn offers a refreshing take on open‑world shooting with a distinctive personality and rewarding gameplay loop.

🌈 1. Striking Post‑Apocalyptic World

One of New Dawn’s most notable strengths is its lively, colorful vision of a post‑apocalyptic Hope County. Rather than the drab color palette many associate with post‑nuclear settings, the world is rich with neon flora, energetic landscapes, and memorable landmarks reclaimed by nature. This creative aesthetic gives the game a unique identity and keeps exploration exciting from start to finish.

The world feels alive and dynamic, with random encounters and evolving enemy control that encourage continual engagement and discovery.

🔫 2. Fast‑Paced and Satisfying Combat

Combat in Far Cry New Dawn is consistently fun and thrilling. Gunplay is tight and responsive, and the mix of firearms, improvised weapons, and explosives keeps combat varied. Enemy encounters are smartly designed, often forcing players to adapt on the fly using tactics rather than brute force.

The game also introduces new enemy types and mechanics that differentiate it from previous entries, making each firefight feel fresh even for series veterans.

🛠️ 3. Rewarding Progression and Crafting

New Dawn takes the Far Cry progression systems and fine‑tunes them into a more meaningful and engaging experience. The base building and crafting mechanics give players a sense of ownership over their outpost, while collecting resources and upgrading equipment feels satisfying and impactful.

The Homebase and Outpost mechanics create strategic reasons to explore and defend territory, encouraging players to invest in their world as much as their character.

🤝 4. Strong Co‑Op and Social Play

A welcome feature is the seamless co‑op integration, which lets players team up with friends (or match with others online) and tackle missions together. The cooperative experience is both chaotic and rewarding — coordinating attacks, sharing gear, and clearing outposts makes for memorable play sessions.

Co‑op gives New Dawn added longevity and makes its open world feel all the more lively and social.

📜 5. Character and Tone With Personality

New Dawn strikes a unique narrative tone — lighter and more irreverent than its predecessor — while still maintaining stakes that keep the story moving. Characters are colorful and often humorous without feeling shallow, and the antagonists bring flair and memorable moments that fuel the game’s personality.

Rather than taking itself too seriously, the story embraces fun and weirdness where appropriate, and that balance enhances the overall experience.

🏁 Final Thoughts

Far Cry New Dawn may not reinvent the wheel, but it builds on a solid foundation with confidence, style, and fun. Its distinctive world design, compelling combat, rewarding progression, and engaging co‑op make it a standout adventure for fans of open‑world shooters.

Whether you’re a long‑time franchise fan or new to the series, New Dawn offers a lively, enjoyable journey that’s both familiar and refreshingly bold.

Overall: ⭐ 8 / 10 — A vibrant, action‑packed open‑world experience that revitalizes the Far Cry formula with flair and heart.

This is a game that was engineered for micro-transactions and literally every aspect of this game suffers from this decision.  It feels like a game that was more inspired by Candy Crush and badly-done Borderlands than Far Cry.  Let me explain:

1.) This is fairly obvious after 30 seconds of playing, but this is not the usually polished Far Cry title.  Far Cry 3/4/5 are extremely polished games --but not here.  There's little control glitches, horrifically stupid AI, and highly unpolished mechanics everywhere.

2.) The game designers randomly shoe-horn in RPG elements. This wasn't done with the player in mind, this was done to turn the grindiness knob all of the way to 100 to "encourage" the player to pay Ubisoft micro-transactions to give you the experience you actually want, i.e. a game without all of the grindy garbage. Let me explain in further points.

3.) Basic game mechanics that you used to have --the game automatically spawning vehicles near bases so you can commute quickly, fast travel to bases, being able to purchase upgrades to vehicles/weapons in in-game currency-- are all striped out and modified.  In order to have any of these things, you know suddenly need to start collecting like 50 different types of in-game currency.  There map is nearly devoid of vehicles, you can walk around 10 minutes without finding one.   So you want to spawn vehicles at a base?  Well, you need to first go through enough missions to "purchase" a vehicle station at your base with a specific kind of currency.  Okay, great, so I did that --now I get a vehicle?  No, obviously not.  Now you need to provide a big chunk of a different rare currency in order to "build" the vehicle. New Dawn is, as of writing this review, the most recent entry in the Far Cry series. Honestly, despite how much I love this series, I think this game would be a hard sell to anyone who isn't already a fan of the series. As a spin-off followup to Far Cry 5, it feels like it makes unnecessary changes and took away some of the wrong ideas from FC5. Some additions and changes are good, but others are just completely baffling on so many levels.

I have to address the most obvious and most baffling change first: the proto-RPG combat system. Weapons and enemies are tiered. You need level 2 weapons to dish out a good amount of damage to level 2 enemies, level 3 weapons for level 3 enemies, and so fourth. This only serves to make the shooting feel so much worse. Weapons in general don't hit as hard as they do in the rest of the series, and certain weapon types are completely absent in some tiers. If you like your double barrel shotguns, you'll miss them in the late-game. You'll need to dump well over a mag from a level 2 weapon into a level 3 enemy, which makes the enemies feel like artificial bullet sponges.

Leading off of this point is the fact that weapon customization is outright gone. Did you like the lever-action rifle from Far Cry 5? Too bad - it's gone here! Did you like the silenced pump-action from the rest of the series? Too bad - it's only going to remain viable for several hours! This total absence of weapon customization seems baffling to me. You have to choose from a series of preset weapons, so you'll no longer feel like your weapons are truly yours.

This game also tries to stretch out its playtime by having a lot of repetitive or drawn-out content. The game wants you to continually replay outposts and expeditions (which are side missions taking place in large but isolated regions). The outposts actually seem pretty well designed, but the expeditions provide some problems. Even if you perfectly stealth-pacifist your way through it, enemies will spontaneously psychically lock onto your position shortly after you complete the primary objective. This just seems like a contrived excuse to draw these missions out and/or punish stealth players.

I've been horrifically negative so far, so I'll acknowledge some genuine good points: Takedown animations are far more brutal and satisfying than they were in FC5. They have so much more weight and impact that I'd argue they're the best in the series. Outposts are still a ton of fun, despite the game's annoying insistence to keep replaying each outpost for more resources. The double-jump you acquire late into the game is a ton of fun, but it feels a little underutilized in the level design. Elite (max level) enemies provide a really fun challenge, and they gave me some of the most intense battles in the entire franchise.

I'm also quite fond of the environments. The world is actually pretty pleasant to the eyes. There's no denying that this game has a ton of color to it. Expeditions take you to unique locations as well that are extremely visually distinct from the rest of the game. I was really taken by surprise to see the varying swamp, desert, and island environments hidden away in mundane side content.

Do I recommend this game? Not to anyone who isn't already a Far Cry fan. There's a lot of poor design choices in this game that feel like they outnumber the good ones. I originally had mixed feelings about Far Cry 5, but I think this game  made me appreciate FC5 a lot more. Ultimately, I'd only suggest getting this game on sale. It's alright, but it's easily the worst take on this formula in the series.

Compared to Far Cry 5:

- "same" map, but really feels like it's a new one due to drastical changes in the environment. Some sections are cut off, so the map size is maybe two thirds of that in FC5
- fewer people, more (mutated) animals
- fishing is still in
- drugs are out
- can have only one companion instead of two
- no boats and planes roaming around, so you can finally hike/fish in peace
- two crazy black women instead of two crazy white dudes as antagonists
- you are not the "hero" this time, rather his independent agent
- there is a very simplistic RPG system here with 4 tiers (normal, rare, epic, legendary) for weapons and NPCs. Although it's arguably unnecessary, it leaves the "one shot, one kill" gameplay of the Far Cry series intact, while giving the player a little more sense of direction and progression. It mostly forces you to gather some materials and then commit to an upgrade choice, unless you want to grind more materials and craft other high tier weapons as well.
- all points of interest can be completed by gathering all the materials on their site. While this is a nice functional addition to POIs / map progression, it can be very frustrating when you are a completionist and bad at searching props
- some gameplay aspects are now embodied in your upgradeable base. Gather materials to upgrade facilities, which then improve your stats (like health) or unlock quick travel via helicopter, craft vehicles in the garage, add map markers at the cartographer
- of COURSE this game has outposts to conquer. Difference here is, after conquering you can either keep it as a respawn/crafting station, or abandon it; this will then repopulate it with enemies of the next higher tier
- expeditions: you can travel to some completely new locations and usually steal something from the bad guys. Maps I've seen so far were an abandoned aircraft carrier, giving me huge FC1 vibes, and a spooky post-apocalyptic amusement park. Each expedition also comes in multiple tiers, if you're up for some grind.
- skinning: While in Far Cry 3, skins were used to craft items directly, in Far Cry 5, they were just converted into money. New Dawn is a middle ground, where you convert skins into materials and then use those for crafting. It works well as long as you can ignore the idiotic idea that Elk Hide produces Duct Tape and Wolfskin produces Copper
- experts: much like in FC Primal, you have to find experts before you can upgrade facilities to certain tiers. The associated quests are pretty fun

All in all, New Dawn is a fully fledged game and a worthy entry to the series. It looks like it acts as somewhat of a guinea pig for trying out (or leaving out) game mechanics as little mutations (hehe) to the FC game formula. FC5 is still the greater title and should ideally be played first, as  New Dawn is the direct successor and many of the characters make reappearances.

I wish there was a "middle ground" option for reviews. Far Cry: New Dawn is a game that excels in some areas and utterly fails in others. It addresses some of Far Cry 5's issues but creates new ones as well. It's very grindy and intent on making you use microtransactions to gain an edge against your enemies (I would strongly recommend not buying into them, though). At the core of this bizarre mashup of Borderlands, Fallout, and Far Cry is an entertaining open world FPS buried by questionable development choices.

Taking place 17 years after the..."conversation-starting" Resist Ending of Far Cry 5, Hope County has been reduced to a nuclear wasteland. You play as the security captain of a nationwide militia arriving to help with the rebuilding effort. However, your train is ambushed by the Highwaymen, an anarchist group dedicated to looting settlements for their own gain. Cut off from your team, your character allies with the citizens of Sanctuary and New Eden to drive out the Highwaymen once and for all.

The greatest strengths of Far Cry games are their charismatic villains and their engrossing environments. New Dawn lacks both of these. The main villains of ND have no defining philosophy beyond "we get to take your stuff," and the map is just recycled from Far Cry 5. Some characters from FC5 return, but they're either reduced to minor roles (Grace, Father Jerome, The Deputy) or limited to references in journal entries (Tracy, Nadine). Fan favorites like Jess Black aren't even referenced at any point. Even Joseph Seed is made underwhelming in this game! It's disappointing how Far Cry 5's compelling cast of varied characters got shafted in favor of an unimpressive new cast. As for the environments, expedition missions to cool areas like a beached frigate and an airplane crash in the woods add some variety, but they're fairly limited overall.

Combat in New Dawn takes on an RPG-like approach, where enemies have different levels and health values. Weapons have ranks that determine their damage and, more importantly, how resistant enemies are to them. Lower-level guns are made useless against high-level enemies, forcing you to grind for better equipment. You can't customize guns here, but New Dawn does a good job of making FC5's collection of weapons feel unique. New attachments like bayonets are equipped to some weapons. Existing attachments get a more improvised appearance, like oil cans taking the place of silencers. The weapons also look heavily maintained and feel fitting for a post-apocalyptic environment. 

There are also some fun and ridiculous abilities you get over the course of the game, like double-jumping and going into a berserker mode to deal more damage. Knife takedowns also make a grisly return, though they are much slower than they were in previous games. It's tough to chain takedowns when your character takes so much time performing a single knife execution. On the bright side, bayonet takedowns exist and go quicker than normal ones.

Getting new guns/vehicles and upgrading the installations at Sanctuary require you to find and scavenge resources. You can do this by hunting, raiding Highwayman supply drops, and replaying outpost missions with stronger opponents. This can require a LOT of grinding to get through. Naturally, Ubisoft hands you a small amount of microtransaction coins here and there to tempt you into buying your way to victory. The microtranscations here are more prevalent than they were in Far Cry 5 (which mostly purchased outfits and weapon reskins), and the way they're promoted feels sleazy.

Far Cry 5 had a fantastic soundtrack. so topping it would be a near-impossible task. New Dawn has some good tracks (like its main theme and the map menu music), but its soundtrack is mostly forgettable. It's nice that the Highwaymen have their own songs to set them apart from FC5's cult, at least.

Would I recommend Far Cry: New Dawn by itself? No. However, there are mods that remove the damage resistances and other grind-encouraging mechanics to make the game more enjoyable. I would personally recommend the Scavenger Mod and the Improved Weapons mod (bundled with the Unreleased Variety mod) to make lower-level guns viable and unlock content that wasn't made available. These mods bring it close to the fun, frantic action of Far Cry 5, and turn its RPG elements into less of a chore and more of an enhancement to the overall experience.

Overall, Far Cry: New Dawn feels like a wasted opportunity. We could have had a full-blown Vietnam War DLC instead of this half-baked continuation of Far Cry 5's story. Weak villains and greedy design choices bog down the fun gameplay of the franchise in this spin-off. If you still want to play it, I would wait until it is at least 50% off on sale, and I would install the previously mentioned mods to get around its less-than-fun enemy damage resistances.

My rating: 7.5/10

[h1]In-Depth Analysis[/h1]
[h3]Pros[/h3]
[b]1.[/b]
Exploring the post-apocalyptic Montana really feels like a lively, dynamic experience thanks to the numerous random events that can happen regularly. Resource convoys, enemy patrols, gunfights between various factions and brutal animal packs, are all factors that can influence a mission or side activity at any time. Generally the encountered NPCs react realistically to such events, as well.

[b]2.[/b]
Weapon feeling, sounds and impacts feel satisfying and realistic against the enemy: grenade launchers have foes fly away, same goes for point-blank shotguns, while more exotic weapons have custom effects like setting things on fire or ricochet ammo, lock-on missiles. The arms variety is good, with options for also stealth if needed. Enemies have average AI and will use cover, grenades often. 

[b]3.[/b]
Just a few shots from an average bandit are all it takes to down a player on the toughest setting. When it comes down to Elite enemies or animals, they may very well one-shot the protagonist(s) there and then, depending on the situation. Using ramshackle weapons against higher-level foes incurs in heavy damage penalties, further adding to the difficulty especially early on.

[b]4.[/b]
Side and main-missions that involve specific characters or treasure hunts all feel unique, and have their own little "mini-stories" to discover, for those that want to take time reading lore documents. Not only that, but often these operations feature unique puzzles, gameplay elements or situations that force to change approach radically.

[h3]Cons[/h3]
[b]1.[/b]
Except for the last story chapter, the rest of FCND's adventure proves utterly mediocre and unremarkable as far as good stories are concerned. The stereotyped "chaotic evil" villains don't have an ounce of charisma, same goes for the various NPCs that mostly try to be amusing / stand out, only to end up being cringe at best.

[b]2.[/b]
Exception made for Treasure Hunts, all other side-activities, in particular "loot zones" and outposts, become a real chore in the long run. Each enemy outpost can be captured then abandoned again to face a harder version of it - that doesn't change much though, apart from rewards and enemy scaling. This has to be done many times to get all the upgrades.

[b]3.[/b]
Once top-tier weapons and a good amount of perks are acquired, the difficulty drastically lowers, simply because most enemies will be obliterated instantly by such mighty weapons or armed vehicles. In particular armed helicopters are a huge abuse, since they can clear entire outposts without enemies even being able to shoot back. 

[b]4.[/b]
Only the lobby host will be able to upgrade the base facilities, get certain story-related perks or initiate fast-travel and other interactions. Progress in the story is not saved for the eventual co-op partner, only resources are. This becomes frustrating because the second player will basically have no place to invest their share of the earnings, and be locked out of some progression skills as well.

[h1]Gameplay Breakdown[/h1]

[b]Exploration[/b]
Is performed on foot or with the use of ground, sea and air vehicles such as cars, jeeps, boats and helicopters. Progressively better and faster vehicles can be unlocked at the garage after the proper upgrades have been performed to the home base. The world is rather large and dotted with points of interest, secondary quests and secret areas - most of them can be found manually or located by buying the relative map from traders, for a price in Ethanol, one of the main currencies. Mostly, exploration involves travelling from point A to point B in order to clear the next point of interest.

[b]Combat[/b]
Plays out in an FPS fashion, with players eventually be able to carry one sidearm, two main weapons and a heavy one, plus a variety of throwables like grenades, molotovs, C4 charges and knives. Melee weapons are also an option, although not recommended in most cases, ranged ones are just better. Enemies come in different archetypes like snipers, assault troops, melee specialists and so on, differing in level as the game progresses. Animals use the same system, there are some rare ones whose pelts can be traded for great amounts of resources. Armed vehicles are a thing later on, they are overpowered mostly and make fights very easy.

[b]Side Activities[/b]
Comprise quests, treasure hunts and some collectible hunting as well. The locations are sparse and often difficult to find, however the trader maps completely remove this hardship. The puzzles required to complete hunts and collectible finds are enjoyable and in the first case, unique for each instance. The rewards are really good too, so totally worth doing.

[b]Character Progression[/b]
Mainly comes from perk and weapon unlocking. Passive skills are unlocked with points granted by completing challenges, this encourages taking part into varied activities and using different weapon types or other means to kill enemies. Weapons are unlocked at specific benches at one's home base, each "bench level" upgrade enables crafting a new roster of weapons using the crafting materials acquired during missions. The same system is used for vehicles, consumables and ammunition types.

[b]Expeditions[/b]
Are external missions, oriented towards stealth, that see players engage into "heists" of sorts against fortified Highwaymen outposts. As soon as they are discovered, and endless stream of enemies will converge on players, which happens anyway once the package is acquired. The ultimate goal is to escape to the extraction helicopter with the loot, within the allotted time.

It's a much shorter game with way less content that they attempt to mask with 'scaling' content that gets harder each time you run through it (such as the outposts). And I think this is where the problems lie. It's just too short, with around 12-14 hours of actual gameplay.

For the most part, it's the same as FC5 but with worse story, an altered (but similar) map, and a couple of revised systems. So have a read of [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/frostbladestorm/recommended/552520/]my review [/url]of FC5 to get a baseline as I'll just go over the changes.

+ Expeditions. The best part of the game. You can do short missions to unique environments that I found very engaging. While they are simple, they're quite fun.

- Weapon Customisation. They dropped it entirely.
- Vehicles. The selection is rubbish with very little variety.

Overall, I wouldn't recommend it over 5 and I'd only suggest playing it if you have played 5. It's a step back, but I'm still glad to have played it. 5.5/10.

I finished Far Cry New Dawn in 8.5 hours and it honestly feels like nothing more than an epilogue — basically a story DLC for Far Cry 5. It follows the events after FC5, sure… but it doesn’t offer what Far Cry 5 did.

The story isn’t engaging, the finale is way too straightforward and lacks any intelligence, and the last fight felt like I was playing some weird Far Cry 4 “Yeti DLC” again. From a narrative perspective, the whole thing comes off like it was made by fan modders rather than a proper mainline entry.

I bought it on sale for under 5€, and that’s the only price point where I can recommend it. Anything more makes no sense.

What annoyed me the most was the grinding: upgrading homebase stations, leveling gear, weapons locked behind levels, and then still having to farm crafting resources on top of that. It’s just busywork.

Flying also isn’t available here, the map is small, and even the road infrastructure feels weak — like the world isn’t built for fun movement the way other Far Cry games are.

Overall it’s a 6/10. For me it’s better than Far Cry 2, but it doesn’t even come close to the other entries. Maybe Far Cry Primal is slightly better than New Dawn too. I only recommend it if you want to see what happened after Far Cry 5’s ending — and I’m definitely not playing this again.

[b]Note: This review contains spoilers for Far Cry 5. If you have not yet completed that game, it is highly recommended that you do so before continuing reading this review. You have been warned.[/b]

Ever since Far Cry 3, we've gradually been conditioned to expect a .5 release between titles in Ubisoft's flagship solo/co-op FPS franchise; Blood Dragon, Primal, and now New Dawn are all part of the mid-series releases that serve to tide us over until the next insanity-filled full-length campaign can be unleashed unto the world. All of these games are reskins of their base release, and Far Cry New Dawn shows that more prominently than any of its previous counterparts as it's still set in rural Montana, only 17 years after the events of its parent, Far Cry 5.

In a turn of events that are brand new to the franchise, Far Cry New Dawn solidifies which ending was canonical for its parent title. Known as the 'good ending', Far Cry 5 ended with the beginning of a nuclear fallout, as Joseph Seed called down damnation onto the earth; an event which would come to be known as The Collapse. The residents of Hope County all took refuge underground, where they stayed waiting out nuclear winter for nearly two decades. Emerging some 17 years later, they find that the land has flourished beautifully in the absence of humanity, and they rebuild a home which they name Prosperity. Though not all is good and peaceful in the new world, as they come to find out. A horrible gang known as the Highwaymen, led by vivacious and vicious twin sisters, Mickey and Lou, burn, pillage, and annihilate everything and everyone in their path. What's more is that the remaining members of Eden's Gate have rebuilt as well, and Joseph Seed remains their ringleader.

Don't let the cover art and promotional propaganda fool you; Mickey and Lou are only a very, very small part of the New Dawn story. They're present even less than Pagan Min was in Far Cry 4, and their main interaction is mostly via radio chatter as you scurry about your missions and item plundering. The first half of the campaign will kind of involve them, though you'll instead be liberating outposts, rescuing captured characters to help Prosperity grow, and recruiting designated people for your roster team like in the base game. After that point, the story is entirely focused on Joseph Seed and his little cult. The gameplay heavily revolves around scavenging resources so that you can upgrade Prosperity several times over, including a bunch of infrastructures such as the garage, weapon bench, and infirmary. In fact, aside from liberating outposts over and over again to gain the valuable resource known as Ethanol, which is used for upgrading, the biggest time sink of this entire release is scavenging.

Where both Blood Dragon and Primal set out to create entirely new worlds, stories, and gameplay styles, New Dawn is a tried and true rehash of Far Cry 5. Everything here is the same, with the exception that the landscape is filled with more vibrant neon pink and blue structures. Oh, and there's a sick new weapon called the Sawblade. Everything else is the same, and you'll even be encouraged to go to old landmarks with pre-apocalypse photos and line up the before-and-after shots. It's far from an interesting concept, and it feels as though Ubisoft took the laziest, money-grubbing route possible this time around. Primal in and of itself looked and felt nothing like Far Cry 4, and that title can stand on its own. New Dawn is just a more colorful rural Montana, with many of the same characters, and a lot of cringey tacked-on humor that just isn't well-received. Perhaps if the developers took more time to add substance to the gameplay, instead of chocking it full with item-hunting filler, there could've been a chance for this game to earn some well-needed individuality.

So far we've established that Far Cry New Dawn is one of the expected half-way releases between major titles in the franchise, that it's neither a great game nor a particularly poor one, but it's the most inferior of all the other spin-offs. If it's so mediocre, why not a half-hearted recommendation? Well, ladies and gentlemen, in typical Ubisoft fashion, this game is filled to the rafters with bugs. Not your usual ones where reloading a save will make it all better; there are those too, but wait... there's more! There are still day one game breaking bugs that Ubisoft are completely aware of, and refuse to fix; coupled with invaluable advice from their support such as "just start a new game". There are also treasure hunts that can become permanently glitched out, locking achievement hunters out of their precious rewards. If you enjoy spending 15-20 hours progressing through a campaign, only to be potentially blocked completely with zero hope of a fix at the halfway point in the story, then by all means... this release may be what you're looking for. If this is the kind of BS that infuriates you, no discount will make this game worth purchasing.

Even without the game breaking problems that have just celebrated their first birthday, Far Cry New Dawn is uninspired. Ubisoft really thought that they could woo audiences with pretty colors, and that may have worked for some people. For the rest of us, treking through rural Montana yet again, to mostly scavenge items for upgrades and do very little else just isn't that fun. The game has its moments, but they're few and far between. Even further between if you're forced to restart your entire game, like I was, right when the plot was starting to get good. That's 15 hours of my life I'll never get back, but it's not the first time Ubisoft has robbed me of life essence. If you're committed to knowing the outcome of Joseph Seed and his cult, this game should run you no more than $20; Ubisoft put no effort into it, so you shouldn't put much of your money into it, either.

I enjoyed the game, but not sure why it wasn't a large DLC or Season Pass for Far Cry 5.  The storyline starts with you on a train that crashes in a post-apocalyptic world, and the action starts right away.  You are saved by a group of folks who live out in a safe area called Prosperity, and the highwaymen led by the Twins are after you.  For some reason that storyline really sucks, but once you get further into the story it has its own story within the story that really works well as a sequel to Far Cry 5.

If this is what an apocalyptic world looks like, then let's drop the bombs.  The world is beautiful.  The sky has colors like northern lights.  The flora of the area is bright and vivid.  Animals look rugged and sometimes brighter than they should be.  It's a beautiful world to explore and this is where Far Cry has always shined as a game, the exploration is a blast.  The world doesn't look all that much different than the previous game, but following creeks, running through the forest, or eventually squirrel diving through the air to cover more ground is stunning no matter where you are.  The scenery does not change all that much, though certain sections are definitely more swampy than foresty.

The action is good, not great, but good.  You get to craft weapons as you collect resources by killing people and taking over bases.  There are a wide variety of melee weapons and a variety of guns including objects you can lob too.  The action started out easy and worked well by progressing towards a much more difficult enemy.  The enemies themselves did not vary too often.  While there are animals to fend off as well as highwaymen, the majority of the time you will be killing highwaymen and they kind of all look the same.  As the storyline progresses enemies are harder to kill unless you have the upgraded weapons, and it makes for much more intense battles as you try to conquer another outpost.

You have the option to purchase perks like access to upgraded weapons, being able to move around silently, silent kills, and more.  Eventually, you get access to weird out of this world, a la Far Cry: Blood Dragon, type of perks like double jump and other additional perks.  The game is the same as all other Far Cry games, you can play the missions only, or you can venture and hit up all of the areas on the map and collect all of the resources you can, discover all of the prepper shelters for added collectibles.  The one new resource that I don't think existed in the previous game is that now ethanol is a key component to upgrades to your base, crafting certain weapons, and more.  You can find random plane drops for ethanol, that you typically will have to fight for when you find them.  You can find some by highjacking an ethanol truck and bringing it back to an outpost without blowing up.  Even highjacking them without blowing it up before trying to make it back to an outpost before being shot and have the enemies blow it up was difficult at first.  Or, you can take over outposts.

Outposts are areas with a large contingent of highwaymen.  You shoot your way in, or silently take them out one by one until you take it over.  If they see you and they sound the alarm, reinforcements will arrive and just make it frustratingly more difficult than it should have been.  Once you take over an outpost, you can get some extra ethanol by giving it back to the highwaymen.  Taking it over a second or even a third time keep increasing the difficulty of taking over the outpost.  But each time, you will get more ethanol.  Increasing the difficulty once you have the appropriate weapons to even try it was quite fun and really amped up the ante on the intense stealth or intense shoot outs.

Eventually, you do need to collect a lot of resources in order to upgrade your base, which then allows you to upgrade you skills like crafting better weapons.  You cannot win this game without upgrading, which means it requires a bit of grinding.  While it took me quite some time to beat, I was collecting quite a lot more than I would have needed, and I think that easily you could finish the game in less than 20 hours, or take as long as me and almost 100% the entire game.

If you like the Far Cry series, then this will feel just right.  If you liked Far Cry 5, then I would suggest that this is a must as it really is a good sequel storywise.  There's not much that's new to the series, but hey if it's fun, why not give it a shot.  I definitely recommend it.  Now to wait for Far Cry 6 on Steam.

What can I say about 'Far Cry: New Dawn'?

If I'm being honest with myself, it's an expansion for 'Far Cry 5' that was bloated and padded to the fullest extent in order to justify inflating the price.

Does that make it a bad game? No, I don't think so.

Is it worth it at full price? No, I don't think so either.

Don't get me wrong. There's plenty to like about this title. The visuals, with a colorful spin on a post-nuclear wasteland, are quite nice. Some new weapons, vehicles, and perks at your disposal are genuinely fun to use and experiment with. The open world is intriguing and makes you want to dive deeper and explore its ruins and crevices. All in all, it's not bad at all.

However, the truth is that the sweet stuff that makes 'Far Cry'...well...'Far Cry'...just isn't here.

First and foremost, the villains are uninspired and boring. The series has made a name for itself with its antagonists, who are always full of charisma, personality, or so crazy they're compelling. The villains here, the "Twins", are so generic and dull. Not to insult the performances of the actresses, but their characters just aren't up to par.

Leading us into the greater story. While there are moments of glaring potential, where I was actually interested in what was happening (specifically in Act 2), 'New Dawn' somehow drops the ball and doubles down on the dreadfully generic story beats. Are you hoping to see more of Joseph Seed and his New Eden, like I was? Well, you'll get to spend all of ten minutes with them before the game decides to pivot straight back into the dreadfully boring conflict with the Twins and their goons. I cannot understate how disappointing the story is here.

Lastly, as I mentioned before, the padding is so blatant and ham-fisted. The game expects you to fully upgrade you home base by the end of the storyline, but forces you to collect an ENORMOUS amount of resources to do so. While this could have been interesting if the resources needed were diverse and had more ways to collect them, you are required to collect ONE universal resource. ONE. You'll be collecting this mainly by liberating outposts. Yes, this is a signature 'Far Cry' mechanic. However, the game expects you to RECAPTURE an outpost you've already liberated in order to collect MORE resources. It quickly sucks the fun out of anything to do with outposts and other content. This was nothing short of a slap in the face for long-time 'Far Cry' players, like myself.

With all that being said, 'Far Cry: New Dawn' is something that had so much potential that elected to waste in favor of nudging players towards its in-game cash shop (it's Ubisoft, after all).

If you really need more 'Far Cry', wait for a sale.

If not, just skip this one.

I can’t support the addition of a health bar system in a Far Cry game. Landing a clean headshot only for it not to be a one shot kill completely kills the experience for me. It undermines what the series used to do so well grounded, immersive gunplay that rewarded precision. The RPG style mechanics, including enemy levels and damage numbers, feel completely out of place and take away from the raw, chaotic realism the series thrived on. The antagonists are also not interesting at all. When you compare them to characters like Vaas Montenegro or Pagan Min, the difference is night and day. Those characters had presence, personality, and unpredictability. Here, the villains feel flat and forgettable, lacking the charisma that helped carry earlier games. Even the story as a whole struggles to stay engaging, often feeling like a loose framework rather than something worth investing in. This experience is a big part of why I haven’t even tried Far Cry 6. I really don’t like the direction the series is taking. And that’s coming from someone who was blown away by Far Cry 3 when the formula was still fresh it was an incredible game that I still go back to from time to time. Back then, the open world felt interesting and I felt a need to explore, here, it feels more repetitive, with side activities and outposts lacking the same sense of tension or creativity.

The color scheme also feels forced. While it can look beautiful at times, it often becomes sensory overload, especially during chaotic encounters. There are moments where the art direction shines, but it doesn’t always serve the gameplay. The new improvised, Fallout style weapons feel gimmicky and inconsistent. They sound fun in theory, but in practice, they lack impact and reliability especially when compared to the standard weapons, which just feel better to use overall. Even the progression system feels off. Instead of naturally improving your character through skill and equipment, it leans too heavily on arbitrary upgrades and grinding. This slows the pacing and makes encounters feel artificially stretched out. Coop can add some fun, but it doesn’t fix the core design issues. That said, it’s not without its positives. The world is still visually striking in places, and the sense of building and growing your community is one of the more rewarding aspects of the game. It adds a layer of progression that was missing in earlier entries, even if it’s not enough to carry the experience.

My god Ubisoft Montreal, what happened?
The opening was promising enough, with some kind of Mad-Max style villains with some interesting visuals and what seemed like a decent cast of characters. But that is legitimately where my praise for the story ends. This game's story is abysmal. The only characters I liked were Joseph Seed (a character from Far Cry 5 just pasted into this one's story), Nick Rye (who has next to no part to play in the story but I liked him in Far Cry 5) and maybe Rush (but he didn't really get all that much of an opportunity for characterization). As for the other characters (Kim Rye, Carmina Rye, Ethan, etc.) they were all really poorly-written. Carmina comes across like she might have something important to do in the story, but she is literally not involved with any main mission besides the first. The same goes for Kim Rye, all she ever does is shout at you over a radio occasionally, giving you objectives seemingly at random, and doing little else besides. Rush could have been an interesting character, I think, if he hadn't been executed by the twins two hours after you meet him. Why did they do that? They give you no reason to care about Prosperity at all, and then they kill off the character who possibly could have remedied that. Fair play Ubisoft, but please do warn squeamish people next time you're about to shoot yourself in the foot like that.

As for the dialogue: I was tolerating how bad-to-mediocre it was at first, but then it really started grating my nerves, so I turned down the voice volume, turned on subtitles, and put on a podcast when exposition was going on. It was honestly that annoying to me, I swear. It's all either matter-of-fact, cut-and-dry exposition, or cringe-humor that tries to relate to "these kids nowadays". As an example of the latter: this one character in a white lab-coat (who you only meet once and never speak to again) sends you down into the old Eden's Gate bunker that you assault and destroy in Far Cry 5. Now, this really could have been an interesting moment to walk in the footsteps of the deputy, and to connect, on a deeper level, to the lore of the other game. Now, it really COULD have been that, but what is it instead? Oh, it's just spelunking into the bunker while you're being shouted at by a personified tumblr "LOL XD RANDEM" post the whole way down. No dramatic tension or reverent tone for the relics you're uncovering, just a bunch of gut-wrenchingly awful "jokes". They completely ruin the tone of several moments with pitiful attempts at humor. It legitimately makes me want to uninstall the game every time anyone makes a quip.

The gunplay is fine. There really isn't much more to say, but the gameplay as a whole is honestly frustrating. The RPG-style elements (calling them that feels like an insult to RPG's) they introduced make the game seem really more grindy than it needs to be. It takes literal ages to kill legendary enemies with any weapon besides a legendary one, which, for all my looting and scavenging, I couldn't find a certain part needed to craft any of them. So, needless to say, every legendary enemy I came to slowed the game down to a screeching halt all because I couldn't find the one material I needed to make a legendary weapon. The gameplay has really degraded because of these elements. Now it's not about the awesome stunts and badass moments from the previous game, it's all about upgrading your guns to a different colour grade so you can grind more enemies to make more guns, ad infinitum. It was teeth-grindingly awful.

In conclusion: This was a shit game and even just writing about it gives me a migraine so THE END.

SOME MINOR DETAILS THAT COULD BE CLASSED AS SPOILERS IN REVIEW....



So I was genuinely happy when I finally completed this game, I was glad it was over...
The storyline is extremely short (12 main missions in total!). The game can be completed in around 5 hours if you didn't have to spend time upgrading your base and finding components for better weapons. 
The levelling system in this game is pathetic, the enemies have 4 levels ranging from, I could sneeze and kill them, all the way to unloading over 200 rounds of ammo to remove half of their health bar. 
I know that it is based on the Far Cry 5 map, but this is the most cut down game I have experienced - the number of outposts has been cut down, and the only way to make up for that is by allowing you to essentially hand it back to the enemy so you have to take it down again - with the caveat that the opponents are going to be more difficult the next time you try to take it and you get some base building material from it.
Also, compared to Far Cry 5, stealth is much harder, the enemies can see you much further, can fill up their spotting bar much much faster and their hearing is incredible - this all makes for a frustrating experience if you enjoy playing stealth.
Another issue is that the gun levelling system is stupid, 'oh look ive put some ducktape on a rifle increasing its damage by 100%'. So the level 1 assault rifle will take over 1000 rounds to kill a level 4 standard enemy, stick some tape on it and some plumbing components and suddenly it can take them out in 10 rounds. 

My main issue with this game are the two main protagonists, the Twins, are evil for the sake of being evil. Their actions are utterly bewildering. All other Far Cry leaders have reasons for being evil, Vaas was on drugs and being mentally abused, Hoyt was a slaver. Pagan Min was a dictator and they really spent time on his back story. The only redemption of this story is that it completes the character arc for Joseph Seed (The Father), it wasn't the worst ending for him - but the fight with the Twins is ridiculous - The fight with Ethan is stupid too, and has more in common with Dark Souls than it does with any Far Cry game. 

Positives... I do like the base building aspect but I wish every upgrade visually upgraded the base - I want to see what my hard work has achieved. The specialised loot locations are actually ok, some might dislike it (if they like to discover things while out exploring) because the game tells you where to find these components - personally, it forces me to see places on the map that I would probably never visit. The game is very pretty, very vibrant colours and graphically very impressive- however, the game does stutter quite often (even if running on decent hardware).
Overall, not sure I would even recommend this game even if it were on sale at 90% off - just use that money to buy Far Cry 3/4/5 instead, or use that money to save for Far Cry 6 instead.

Seeing this, after playing Far Cry 3, 4, Primal, 5 and now New Dawn, I'm not buying the next Far Cry release unless these issues disappear from the games:

I totally accept unlocking improved reload speeds via a perk, but this is the fourth Far Cry game where a new player can have the aim of a word-class sniper but must wait enough time to peel, slice, chop and saute an onion for a gun to reload. Put simply: if I have FOUR rounds per clip and I need TWO rounds to kill a Highwayman, how long will it take for me to kill two Highwaymen if I miss a single shot? The answer in Far Cry New Dawn is [b]NaN[/b]. You can't even micro-transact your way out of this limitation. Trust me, I clicked freakin' [i]everywhere[/i] hoping a debit card could speed this lady up.

Protagonist has two hands with opposable thumbs, but somehow can't pop the top of a prescription bottle like their life [i]actually[/i] depends on it. This is the [i]slowest[/i] animation I've ever seen in a Far Cry game. It's so slow, I'm now concerned that past protagonists may have been pill poppers in a prior life. At this rate, the next game may as well just be you fumbling to push through and peel back a blister pack only to drop the pill and have to pick it up, dust it off [i]and then[/i] get your health bar refilled.

This may be an unpopular opinion, but this is the most fun I've had in a Far Cry game since Far Cry Primal was released. I don't know why, but I honestly love the spin-off Far Cry games more than the main ones.

An actual sequel to Far Cry 5, this feels like a stand alone expansion. Post apocalypse Montana isn't that different from the open world of Montana in FC5: just with mutants, radiation, and people LARPing Mad Max in full cosplay with live ammunition. The story takes place years after the ending of 5, though it does give you some follow up and ties up some loose ends. If you were disappointing by the ending of 5, this might make up for that, despite how predictable things tend to get as it seems Ubisoft still uses much of the same formula with their writing.

If there's anything different to be said about gameplay, its that its FC5 with just more options to be ridiculously OP by mid to late game. With the Gifts of Eden you get berserker damage, invisibility, and double jump all while unaccounting for the workbench that lets you craft weapons and upgrade them to absurd amounts of damage. By endgame, with the combination of skills and upgrades, you'll likely have more bullets and rifle rounds on you than the entire US with more missiles than a rogue nation overcompensating for penis envy, while being nearly invisible to most enemies until you decide to finally give them every flavor of death you have. Expeditions make an appearance in this game, which is welcome due to the amount of materials you get from them and can farm them which brings me to one of the drawbacks: the grind. This game is more grindy than FC5, waaaay more. You always have room to increase certain skills, you can always upgrade your guns just a slight more. Sky is the limit with how far you can push your ammunition capacity in addition to weapon damage and throwable capacity. If there is a cap, I sure don't know about it, and I'm already capable of holding dozens of rockets, and thousands of bullets and flamethrower fuel. Once you get to midgame/endgame, it really does feel like just an exercise in how broken you can get.

Do I recommend? Sure, if you don't mind the material grinding. Otherwise its just FC5 with a post apocalypse paint job and super powers.
